title: His Tears Would Do Nothing but Flow
intro: Abu Firas starts by watering a deserted campsite with tears, then recounts a campaign he fought with his cousin Sayf al-Dawla. Ibn Khalawayh's account places the killing of al-Sabbah, Sayf al-Dawla's official at Qinnasrin, before the expedition and puts Abu Firas at the head of a detachment. Sami al-Dahhan dates the campaign to Safar 344 AH (May 955 CE). The poem follows roads and waterholes to the tribes' submission, the prince's pardon and the poet's claim to a share in the victory.

translation: His tears would do nothing but flow,
the fire within his ribs nothing but blaze.
1.sharh: The lover first appears in the third person. Tears and fire seem to have wills of their own, each insisting on the one thing it can do.

translation: The traces of the camp have a claim on me,
a cloud of tears that must miss no day.
2.sharh: He steps into his own account. Revisiting an abandoned campsite creates an obligation much like daily watering, and his tears supply the cloud.

translation: I have spared no effort questioning a dwelling,
but when I asked, it gave no answer.
3.sharh: In an old opening convention, the traveller addresses an abandoned dwelling. His insistence that he has asked often enough makes its silence feel final.

translation: I saw grey hair gleam and welcomed it.
I bade folly and youth goodbye.
4.sharh: Grey hair arrives like a guest who can be greeted. The same greeting dismisses both youth and the behaviour he associates with it.

translation: Age did not turn me grey.
I saw enough from those I loved to do that.
5.sharh: He gives the visible sign of age a different history. The next line makes the loved ones' refusal the cause of his early grey hair.

translation: They sent me a caravan made of cold refusals
and gave it cares to ride.
6.sharh: In this recitation the women's refusals are the riders and his cares are their mounts. The two Arabic words for caravan and mounts are very close in sound.

translation: Have you seen anyone whose neighbour is safer than ours,
whose lands are better defended or greener?
7.sharh: The solitary lover begins to speak as one of a people. Their standing is measured by what a newcomer to their territory can count on.

translation: Ours is the mountain overlooking Nizar.
We occupy its heights and plateaux.
8.sharh: Prestige takes the physical shape of a mountain. Nizar represents the wider Arab kin group over which the speaker claims the high ground.

translation: All people give us precedence, without exception.
They praise our merits without favouritism.
9.sharh: He claims a judgement endorsed by everyone and bought from no one. Two similar-sounding final verbs distinguish making an exception from showing a favourite undue regard.

translation: Rabi'a knows it, indeed all Ma'add,
that we are the head and everyone else the tail.
10.sharh: He widens the body of witnesses from Rabi'a to the larger ancestry of Ma'add. Head and tail translate a genealogical boast into the two ends of a body.

translation: When the reckless men of Ka'b overstepped the bounds,
we opened a door to war between us.
11.sharh: The telling assigns blame to a faction of Ka'b. The speaker's side nevertheless claims the act that opened hostilities, a door deliberately set open.

translation: We gave them the wealth that sustained them.
When they did wrong, we gave them spears.
12.sharh: The same verb governs both gifts. A small change of sound turns the wealth they lived on into the spears with which they are met.

translation: When the Sword of the Faith rose up, we rose,
as if you had roused angry lions.
13.sharh: “Sword of the Faith” designates the poet's cousin Sayf al-Dawla. One man's rising is enough to set the whole band in motion.

translation: We are his spearheads when he meets the thrust of spears,
his blades when he meets the stroke of swords.
14.sharh: The unstated “we” still comes from the preceding line. The men become different parts of their commander's equipment as the fighting changes.

translation: He called us with the spearpoints held out,
and at his summons we were the answer.
15.sharh: Their answer to the call consists in appearing. With the spearpoints already extended, no spoken reply is required.

translation: We are men he fashioned. Our maker excels, so we excel.
A planting thrives because its planter is good.
16.sharh: A patron's protégés were called his “works”. The next half turns something made by hand into something grown, and gives the credit to the same man.

translation: We were like arrows. When they struck
their targets, it was the archer who hit.
17.sharh: His men do the reaching, but a successful shot belongs to the archer. In Arabic the word for their targets almost contains the word for their archer.

translation: They carried us across Ma'an towards al-Jibat,
skirting al-Subayra and al-Qibab.
18.sharh: The itinerary begins from the mounts' point of view. Crossing one place and steering away from two others makes this a line of travel through a named landscape.

translation: They passed al-Badiyya thirsty,
eyeing a mirage where there was no mirage.
19.sharh: Even a mirage would give the thirsty animals something to look towards. His final denial takes away that faintest promise of water.

translation: They crossed Masij when night was a child
and reached Salamiyya when it had gone grey.
20.sharh: Two place names mark the distance and a whole human lifetime measures the night. Dawn goes grey like the poet at the start.

translation: They noticed the mounts only at their steady pace,
clamouring just short of a full charge.
21.sharh: The opponents become aware of the mounts only when they can hear them together. The old gloss locates their pace just below a full run.

translation: The mounts shared praise like spoils for enduring a day
when lives themselves were snatched away.
22.sharh: The mounts share the praise for their endurance as riders might share out spoils. The same root describes the human lives taken on that day.

translation: They called to one another. From every pass came
swift horses picked out for the occasion.
23.sharh: The cry brings animals out of separate passes. Calling them chosen runners gives the gathering force a quality as well as a size.

translation: Nada ibn Ja'far led contingents of Uqayl,
enough to set the mountain gullies flowing around him.
24.sharh: An enemy commander has enough followers to fill the ravines like a torrent. The Arabic for peoples and ravines shares the same three consonants.

translation: Their men were nothing to us but captives,
their possessions nothing but spoils.
25.sharh: The pronoun changes with the reckoning. The men who came with the enemy chief count as prisoners and the property they brought as booty.

translation: As though Nada ibn Ja'far had led them here
as gifts for which he sought no return.
26.sharh: The enemy commander's expedition becomes an absurdly generous visit. Everything has ended up in the speaker's hands with no prospect of anything being given back.

translation: They reinforced their plan with Banu Quray',
and failed, curse them, and so did their plan.
27.sharh: The allies enlisted Banu Quray' to give their plan weight. The plural and then singular ending assign failure first to the people and then to the plan itself.

translation: When the battle grew fierce, it was we
who had the stronger claws and sharper fang,
28.sharh: The angry lions seen rising at their commander's call now have claws and a fang. The sentence holds open for the next line's claims.

translation: whose flank was better guarded, whose neighbour safer,
whose pledge was sounder, whose faults were fewer.
29.sharh: The comparisons continue without a new verb. The speaker moves from power in battle to obligations owed a person who has asked for protection.

translation: With our spears we gave Banu Qushayr a drink
of molten poison in the hollow of al-Uthayr.
30.sharh: The spears offer a drink to Qushayr in a named valley. The image has particular force after a journey spent looking for water.

translation: We drove them on to al-Hayran
as we drive a herd of unruly camels.
31.sharh: The comparison gives the captives an animal's resistance as well as its eventual submission. Repetition of the verb for driving makes the movement continuous.

translation: We turned aside from al-Furuqlus without watering there,
as if we had something against water.
32.sharh: They pass a waterhole without stopping to drink. The speaker lets a decision on the route sound like a strange aversion in people who have known thirst.

translation: They veered from al-Ghuwayr and went on
to the springs of Tadmur and al-Jibab.
33.sharh: The mounts have at last reached actual springs. In the recited sequence this line comes after the two that describe a shower of spears and the crossing of open country.

translation: At Murjahinn they rained down on al-Jibah,
bitter sap poured down in the thrust of spears.
34.sharh: Both names locate the action. The verb “rained” promises relief until the second half gives the bitter substance of this downpour.

translation: They crossed al-Sahsahan with long, quick strides,
carrying us through the open waste.
35.sharh: The mounts carry their riders through a place whose name itself suggests level ground. The two words for striding make their pace palpable.

translation: At al-Samawa we entertained, from the men of Uqayl,
wild beasts of the land and hungry birds.
36.sharh: The language belongs to feeding guests. The unsettling turn is to identify the guests as scavengers and their meal as Uqayl's dead.

translation: For al-Sabbah, and al-Sabbah was a bondsman,
we killed the choicest of their chosen men.
37.sharh: Al-Sabbah's killing helped provoke the campaign. The speaker's pointed contrast of a bondsman and the enemy's elite measures retaliation in the status terms of his own society.

translation: We left in the houses of Banu al-Muhanna
women sobbing aloud in lament.
38.sharh: The account moves inside the enemy's homes. Women's voices replace the sounds of the expedition, giving the victory a cost that can be heard from the other side.

translation: Against Abu Bakr old grudges found satisfaction,
and al-Dibab brought grudges into the open there.
39.sharh: Abu Bakr is a tribal name in this setting. The near repetition in the next half sets a proper name beside an old word for a grudge, suggesting older enmities surfacing again.

translation: We kept Ka'b at a distance for its conduct
and brought Kilab close for its obedience.
40.sharh: Distance and nearness now measure standing with the prince. The tribes receive different treatment according to the conduct the speaker attributes to them.

translation: We scattered Tayyi' towards the Golan
and kept Janab away from its desert range.
41.sharh: The campaign changes where other groups can range. The name Janab comes back almost intact in the verb for keeping it away.

translation: A cloud settled over Uqayl
and dragged a long train over its neighbours.
42.sharh: The cloud is the expedition. Its trailing edge carries trouble beyond Uqayl into neighbouring territory, like a storm reaching places outside its centre.

translation: We rode the horses on towards Numayr,
their bridles straining against our hands,
43.sharh: The horses contribute their own eagerness. Riders and mounts seem to be pulling on opposite ends of the same reins.

translation: with every bold man free in giving his life,
whose injury would cost his kinsmen dear.
44.sharh: The previous sentence acquires its riders. What a man is willing to spend freely is the very life his relatives can least afford to lose.

translation: He had other courses open, yet honour
makes him fear being feared.
45.sharh: The same verb changes voice, from fearing to being feared. The warrior has room to withdraw, yet even the prospect of frightening an opponent out of a meeting troubles his pride.

translation: The man who commands us, whose foes we deal with,
could, if he wished, do our part himself.
46.sharh: The commander is named only after the listener hears what he makes his men do. Delegating the fight becomes an expression of command rather than a mark of dependence.

translation: When they were certain no relief would come,
they called on him for help, and he answered.
47.sharh: Their last possible helper is the man whose forces brought them to this point. His response changes the action from combat to negotiation.

translation: He turned back to kindness towards them, and they returned,
stretching out their necks to whatever he wished.
48.sharh: His return to generosity answers their return to obedience. The exposed necks make visible just how much power the petitioners have conceded.

translation: He sent fear and safety over them in turn,
giving them a taste of honey and bitter sap.
49.sharh: Fear and security can be tasted. Their order reverses in the second half, where honey belongs with safety and bitter sap with fear.

translation: He settled them in al-Jazira when hope had failed,
a man of forbearance when punishment was his to give.
50.sharh: The pardon has a geographical consequence, a place for the defeated to live. Forbearance counts because the prince has complete power to punish.

translation: Their homes, we wrested them away by force.
Their lands, we took them by force.
51.sharh: Each half puts the property first, then doubles down on the act of taking it. The pardon stands beside a plain statement of how the victors obtained control.

translation: Had we wished, we could have barred the desert folk from it,
as woodland lions guard a wood.
52.sharh: The lion image that set the army moving now describes holding territory. The claim of power makes the defeated tribes' continued access sound like a concession.

translation: When other princes send an army
against their foes, we send a letter.
53.sharh: One verb sends both an army and a letter. After recounting an entire expedition, he claims that the family's written word can now do the work of one.

translation: I descend from men who struck at heads long ago
when even the defenders shrank from blows.
54.sharh: The family boast gathers into the single “I”. What earlier generations did when other defenders faltered prepares the poet to ask that his own action be acknowledged.

translation: Did you not know, and a man like you speaks truly,
that I would send it up like a shooting star?
55.sharh: He asks his hearer to vouch for his own part in kindling the conflict. The streak of fire at the close belongs to the man whose inward fire opened the poem.

1.2.2.head: ضُلوع
1.2.2.meaning: Ribs, enclosing the fire in his chest. The Tunisian recension has “his consuming love”.

2.1.3.head: طَلَل
2.1.3.meaning: The remains of a deserted camp, to which the lover owes his tears. Hindawi has “ribs”, carrying over the image from the opening.

2.2.1.head: أَغَبَّ
2.2.1.meaning: To come on alternate days. He undertakes to miss no day of weeping here.

3.1.4.head: تَسآل
3.1.4.meaning: Persistent questioning. Al-Dahhan has “in questioning”, Bencherifa “from questioning”, with the verb “fall short”.

3.1.5.head: رَبع
3.1.5.meaning: A dwelling place, here one once occupied by the people he loved.

3.2.3-4.head: أَجابَ
3.2.3-4.meaning: “It gave no answer.” The campsite is the subject. Hindawi has “I shall receive no answer”, which puts the speaker in its place.

4.2.2.head: الغَوايَة
4.2.2.meaning: Going astray, here the infatuations of youth.

5.2.1.head: رَأى
5.2.1.meaning: To see what has turned him grey. Bencherifa prints “I met with”, making the injury something he encountered.

6.1.3.head: الصُّدود
6.1.3.meaning: Turning away from a lover. The reciter makes the refusals the caravan. In both critical editions it is made of cares.

6.2.4.head: رِكاب
6.2.4.meaning: Riding camels, as distinct from the caravan of riders. In al-Dahhan it is the refusals that serve as mounts.

7.1.5.head: جار
7.1.5.meaning: Someone under a group's protection, a guest or dependant as well as a neighbour.

7.2.2.head: أَمرَع
7.2.2.meaning: Richer in pasture. The reciter places protection before plenty. Bencherifa and Hindawi give them in the reverse order.

7.2.3.head: جَناب
7.2.3.meaning: The ground about a household or settlement.

8.1.5.head: نِزار
8.1.5.meaning: Nizar, son of Ma'add and an ancestor of northern Arabian tribal groupings.

8.2.1.head: حَلَّ
8.2.1.meaning: To settle in a place. One isolated transcription suggests ‘allalna, “we consoled”, and the clip scores better with that word. Both continuous passes, the card and the two critical editions give “we settled”, which fits the uplands and hills.

8.2.2.head: النَّجد
8.2.2.meaning: Raised ground. Hindawi has “glory” in place of “the upland”.

9.1.4.head: حاشى
9.1.4.meaning: To make an exception when applying a judgement.

9.2.4.head: حابى
9.2.4.meaning: To show partiality or grant someone undue favour.

10.1.3.head: رَبيعَة
10.1.3.meaning: Rabi'a, the ancestral grouping that includes Taghlib, the Hamdanids' tribe.

10.1.5.head: مَعَدّ
10.1.5.meaning: Ma'add, Nizar's father in Arab genealogies. Both critical texts have Nizar, and al-Dahhan records Ma'add as a variant.

10.2.2.head: الرَّأس
10.2.2.meaning: The head, contrasted with the tail. The singular makes the group into one body. The Tunisian recension has “the heads”.

10.2.4.meaning: The tail or trailing feathers, an image of subordinate standing.

11.1.5.head: كَعب
11.1.5.meaning: Ka'b, the tribal group whose reckless men the poet blames for starting the conflict.

12.1.2.head: حَريبَة
12.1.2.meaning: Livestock or property on which a household depends. Both critical texts have “choice gifts”.

12.2.2.head: جارَ
12.2.2.meaning: To act unjustly. Al-Dahhan prints “when we wished” and records “when they did wrong”.

13.1.3-4.head: سَيف الدّين
13.1.3-4.meaning: “Sword of the Faith”, here Sayf al-Dawla, Abu Firas's cousin and the Hamdanid ruler of Aleppo.

14.1.1.head: سِنان
14.1.1.meaning: A spearhead. The men are called their commander's spearheads.

14.2.1.head: صارِم
14.2.1.meaning: A sharp sword or cutting blade.

15.1.3.head: مُشرَع
15.1.3.meaning: Held out and levelled, of spears.

16.1.1.head: صَنيعَة
16.1.1.meaning: A protégé whom a patron has advanced or trained.

17.2.1.head: مَرمى
17.2.1.meaning: A target, the point reached by an arrow.

18.1.3.head: الجِباة
18.1.3.meaning: Al-Jibat, a place on the route in al-Dahhan. The Tunisian recension names al-Khiyar.

18.1.5.head: مَعان
18.1.5.meaning: Ma'an, identified in Ibn Khalawayh's route gloss between Masih and Tall Ma'an.

18.2.2.head: الصُّبَيرَة
18.2.2.meaning: Al-Subayra, a place the mounts skirt. Ibn Khalawayh places it beyond Ma'an towards al-Andarin.

18.2.3.head: القِباب
18.2.3.meaning: Al-Qibab, a stopping place on the route. Hindawi has al-Dibab here, the critical editions al-Qibab.

19.1.2.head: البَدِيَّة
19.1.2.meaning: Al-Badiyya, a named stop. Al-Dahhan also records “the wilderness”.

20.1.2.head: ماسِج
20.1.2.meaning: Masij, a place on the route. The reciter's card also gives Masih, the spelling in both critical editions.

20.2.3.head: سَلَمِيَّة
20.2.3.meaning: Salamiyya, a Syrian town east of Hama, reached as dawn begins to show.

21.1.5.head: ثَبات
21.1.5.meaning: A pace just below the full run, as the Diwan glosses it.

21.2.1-2.head: دُوَين الشَّدّ
21.2.1-2.meaning: “Just short of the charge.” The diminutive makes the difference in pace a small one.

21.2.3.head: اِصطَخَبَ
21.2.3.meaning: To clamour, with many voices or noises mixed together.

22.1.1.head: تَناهَبَ
22.1.1.meaning: To share something as spoils. The mounts are the printed subject. Before the following article, the first-person “we shared” can sound identical.

23.1.2.head: اِنبَرى
23.1.2.meaning: To spring forward or come out ready for action.

23.1.5.head: فَجّ
23.1.5.meaning: A wide pass or a way through rising ground.

23.2.2.head: اِنتَجَبَ
23.2.2.meaning: To pick out the best. Al-Dahhan has “for us”, Hindawi and the recitation “for him” or “for it”.

24.1.2-4.head: نَدى بن جَعفَر
24.1.2-4.meaning: Nada ibn Ja'far, a commander of Uqayl opposing Sayf al-Dawla. His name is written Nadi in al-Dahhan and Nada on the reciter's card.

24.1.6.head: عُقَيل
24.1.6.meaning: Uqayl, a branch of Ka'b among the groups opposing the expedition.

24.2.3-4.head: أَسالَ
24.2.3-4.meaning: “They made [the ravines] flow.” The tribal hosts are the subject. Bencherifa’s “he made them flow with them” gives the action to their commander.

24.2.5.head: شِعب
24.2.5.meaning: A ravine or gully in the mountains.

25.2.5.head: نِهاب
25.2.5.meaning: Spoils seized and divided among the victors.

26.2.3.head: راغَ
26.2.3.meaning: To seek or try to secure. He is imagined as seeking no recompense.

27.1.3-4.head: بَنو قُرَيع
27.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Quray', allies called in by the opposing side. Al-Dahhan records Banu Badi' as a variant.

27.2.2-4.head: لا أَبا لَهُم
27.2.2-4.meaning: “May they have no father”, a conventional interruption expressing scorn.

29.1.3-4.head: أَعَزّ جاراً
29.1.3-4.meaning: “Stronger in protecting a neighbour.” Bencherifa has “more bitter to the taste”, describing what an enemy encounters.

29.2.2.head: ذِمَّة
29.2.2.meaning: A binding pledge of protection. The recited wording means “truer to a pledge”. Hindawi describes the pledge as more ample.

29.2.4.head: عاب
29.2.4.meaning: A fault or ground for reproach.

30.1.3-4.head: بَنو قُشَير
30.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Qushayr, a branch of Ka'b named among the opponents.

30.2.1-2.head: بَطن العُثَير
30.2.1-2.meaning: “The hollow of al-Uthayr”, on the campaign route. Al-Dahhan prints al-Ghanthar, Bencherifa al-Uthayr.

31.1.3.head: الحَيران
31.1.3.meaning: Al-Hayran, the destination in the pursuit. The witnesses vary in the pointing of the name, with al-Jiran in Hindawi.

32.1.2.head: الفُرُقلُس
32.1.2.meaning: Al-Furuqlus, a watering place near Salamiyya which the party passes by. Hindawi spells it al-Farqays. Another form in the apparatus is al-Furquns.

32.2.4.head: الماء
32.2.4.meaning: Water, here the watering place they pass. Hindawi has “shelter”.

33.1.3.head: الغُوَير
33.1.3.meaning: Al-Ghuwayr, a place the company veers away from on its way to the springs.

33.2.3.head: تَدمُر
33.2.3.meaning: Tadmur, the oasis city of Palmyra in the Syrian desert.

33.2.4.head: الجِباب
33.2.4.meaning: Al-Jibab, named alongside the springs of Tadmur in the two critical editions and in Hindawi’s text and note.

34.1.2.head: الجِباه
34.1.2.meaning: Al-Jibah, a place on the reciter's card and in Hindawi. Both critical texts have al-Jibat.

34.1.3.head: مُرجَحِنّ
34.1.3.meaning: Murjahinn, glossed here as a place. The same word can describe a heavy, sagging cloud.

34.2.4.head: صاب
34.2.4.meaning: Bitter sap, imagined as the substance of the shower. The same word returns beside honey.

35.1.2.head: الصَّحصَحان
35.1.2.meaning: Al-Sahsahan, a place whose name suggests a broad level tract.

35.1.3-4.head: وَخَدَ
35.1.3-4.meaning: To move at a brisk, lengthened stride, especially of camels.

35.2.1.head: اِجتابَ
35.2.1.meaning: To traverse a stretch of country.

36.1.1.head: قَرى
36.1.1.meaning: To feed a guest. Here the “guests” are animals feeding on the aftermath of fighting.

36.1.2.head: السَّماوَة
36.1.2.meaning: Al-Samawa, the desert region in which this episode takes place.

37.1.1.head: الصَّبّاح
37.1.1.meaning: Al-Sabbah, Sayf al-Dawla's official at Qinnasrin. The prose account connects his killing with the campaign.

37.2.3.head: لُباب
37.2.3.meaning: The choicest part, here the men held in highest standing.

38.1.4-5.head: بَنو المُهَنّا
38.1.4-5.meaning: Banu al-Muhanna, the family to which the Diwan's account assigns leaders on the opposing side.

38.2.1.head: نادِبَة
38.2.1.meaning: A woman who chants a lament for the dead.

39.1.3-4.head: أَبو بَكر
39.1.3-4.meaning: Abu Bakr, a tribal designation in this passage. Al-Dahhan has Banu Bakr as the people taking revenge.

39.2.2.head: الضِّباب
39.2.2.meaning: Al-Dibab, treated as a place by the recording's gloss. The same name is used of a tribe, and the line has several transmitted forms.

39.2.4.head: ضِباب
39.2.4.meaning: Grudges, with a second possible sense of sword edges. The reciter leaves the noun indefinite. Hindawi gives it the definite article.

40.2.3.head: كِلاب
40.2.3.meaning: Kilab, a tribal group of the Banu Amir. Here obedience earns its members favour with the prince.

41.1.1.head: شَرَّدَ
41.1.1.meaning: To scatter or drive away. Both isolated transcriptions suggest a j sound in place of d, and the continuous passes disagree. The printed d and the card give the verb that describes driving Tayyi’ towards the Golan.

41.1.3.head: الجَولان
41.1.3.meaning: The Golan, a region in southern Syria.

41.1.4.head: طَيِّئ
41.1.4.meaning: Tayyi', the tribe the poet says was scattered towards the Golan.

41.2.3.head: جَناب
41.2.3.meaning: Janab, the group kept away from the desert range.

42.1.3.meaning: To settle, as a camel kneels. The critical texts have ma anakha, the recitation qad anakha.

42.2.4.head: ذُناب
42.2.4.meaning: A trailing end of trouble. Hindawi glosses the expression as long days of adversity. The critical texts spell the final word with alif maqsura.

43.1.4.head: نُمَير
43.1.4.meaning: Numayr, a tribe of Banu Amir approached before the settlement. A variant has “we turned” for “we rode on”.

43.2.2.head: عِنان
43.2.2.meaning: A rein held by a rider.

44.1.2.head: مُشَيَّع
44.1.2.meaning: A courageous, stout-hearted man. Al-Dahhan has “before a brave man”, Bencherifa “with every brave man”.

45.2.1.head: هابَ
45.2.1.meaning: To fear. The first verb is active, the rhyming verb passive, “to be feared”.

46.2.1.head: هُمام
46.2.1.meaning: A man of courage and resolution, here Sayf al-Dawla. The isolated sound barely distinguishes humam from imam, “leader”. Both continuous transcriptions give humam, as do the diwans.

47.1.5.head: غِياث
47.1.5.meaning: Relief or rescue. The printed editions and the card give the nominative, with “available to them” understood. The pause leaves the case ending uncertain.

47.2.2.head: المَغوثَة
47.2.2.meaning: Succour. Its Arabic root repeats the cry for relief in the first half. Hindawi has “assistance”, which loses that echo.

48.2.3-4.meaning: “To whatever he wished.” Al-Dahhan prints “to his sword” and records the recited wording in his apparatus.

49.2.3.head: أَري
49.2.3.meaning: Honey, the sweet counterpart to the bitter sap.

49.2.4.head: صاب
49.2.4.meaning: Bitter sap or the plant that yields it, here the taste of fear.

50.1.2.head: الجَزيرَة
50.1.2.meaning: Al-Jazira, Upper Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates, where the defeated are allowed to settle.

50.2.1-2.head: أَخو حِلم
50.2.1-2.meaning: “A brother to forbearance”, someone able to punish who can hold back.

51.1.3.head: اِنتِزاع
51.1.3.meaning: Forcible taking. Al-Dahhan has “by compulsion”, Bencherifa the recited cognate noun.

52.1.3.head: حَمى
52.1.3.meaning: To reserve land by keeping others out of it.

53.1.3.meaning: To dispatch an army, the same verb the speaker uses for a letter. Bencherifa has “roused” or “mobilised” in the first half.

53.2.4.head: كِتاب
53.2.4.meaning: A letter conveying the prince's command.

54.2.3.head: مُحامٍ
54.2.3.meaning: A defender of the people in his charge.

55.2.3.head: بَعَثَ
55.2.3.meaning: To send up or set in motion, here the fire of war. All three printed witnesses have “I would kindle it”.
